b: Paul writes from chains to the first church he planted in Europe, a church that had supported him again and again. He thanks them, updates them, warns them, and asks two quarrelling women to make peace. Words for joy and rejoicing run all through it.

At its centre (2:5–11) is one of the greatest passages about Christ in the New Testament: the one who existed in the form of God ‘emptied Himself’, became a servant, died on a cross, and has been given ‘the name above all names’. Paul holds that up as the pattern for how Christians treat one another.

hist.t: Philippi: a little Rome in Macedonia
b: Philippi was founded by Philip II of Macedon (father of Alexander the Great) about 360 BC, near gold mines, and named after him. In 42 BC the battle of Philippi was fought just west of the city: Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius, Julius Caesar’s assassins, a turning point on the road from republic to empire. Antony settled army veterans there and made it a Roman colony. After Octavian (later the emperor Augustus) defeated Antony in 31 BC, he settled more colonists and renamed it Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensis.

As a colony it had the ‘Italian right’ (ius Italicum): its land was treated as if it were part of Italy, with tax exemptions and the protection of Roman law. Most inscriptions from the 1st and 2nd centuries are in Latin. Its people were proud to be Roman citizens (compare Acts 16:21, 37). This gives point to Paul’s words about conducting yourselves as citizens worthy of the gospel (1:27, where the Greek verb is ‘live as citizens’) and ‘our citizenship is in heaven’ (3:20). There was little Jewish presence; Acts mentions only a riverside ‘place of prayer’, not a synagogue (Acts 16:13).

Excavations have uncovered the forum, theatre, baths, part of the Via Egnatia (the great Roman road east from the Adriatic), and several later churches. A small underground room near one church has been suggested as Paul and Silas’s prison, but the identification is debated. Most visible remains are from the 2nd century or later.

hist.t: Where and when was Philippians written?
b: Paul is in chains (1:7, 13), facing a verdict that could mean death (1:20–23), but he does not say where. Rome (about AD 60–62) is the traditional answer and was almost universally held until the early 20th century. It fits the ‘palace guard’ or Praetorium (1:13), ‘the household of Caesar’ (4:22), the life-or-death stakes (an appeal to Caesar would no longer be possible), and the fairly free house arrest of Acts 28:30–31. Ephesus (about AD 54–57), proposed since 1897, is popular with many scholars today: it is much closer to Philippi, which suits the several journeys the letter implies, and some inscriptions mention praetorian soldiers serving in the province of Asia, though how much this shows is debated. But Acts records no imprisonment in Ephesus (though Paul mentions many imprisonments, 2 Corinthians 11:23). Caesarea (AD 58–60), where Paul was held two years (Acts 24:27), is a third option.
The question is unsettled, and nothing in the letter’s teaching depends on it.

b: That Paul wrote Philippians is almost universally accepted. It names him (1:1), it is intensely personal, and early Christian writers such as Polycarp, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian accepted it without dispute. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, wrote his own letter to the Philippian church in the early 2nd century and reminded them that Paul had written to them.

map.t: Paul’s news: chains that spread the gospel, and life or death
Live worthy of the gospel: united, humble, with the mind of Christ (2:5–11)
Two people to follow: Timothy and Epaphroditus
A warning, and Paul’s story: knowing Christ and the righteousness God gives
Make peace, rejoice, and pray instead of worrying
Thank you for your gift: contentment in Christ

read: Philippians is a letter, written to real people about real events. It was meant to be read aloud to the whole church in one go, so the best way to begin is to read it straight through; it takes about fifteen minutes. Then go back and study it a section at a time.

Like a letter to close friends, it moves between news, thanks, advice and warning. Watch for the words Paul keeps repeating. In our translation, ‘joy’, ‘rejoice’ and ‘glad’ come sixteen times in four short chapters, written from prison. The Greek verb for how we think, or set our minds (phroneō), comes ten times; it lies behind ‘like-minded’ (2:2), ‘Let this mind be in you’ (2:5) and ‘agree’ (4:2). Paul is reshaping how the church thinks, around the mind of Christ.
Paul teaches by example as well as by instruction. He holds up four people for the Philippians to copy: Christ above all (2:5–11), then Paul himself, Timothy and Epaphroditus.

1.t: The confidence is in God's persistence, not ours. Paul writes this to a church he is fond of and cannot visit.
Paul genuinely cannot decide which he would prefer, and settles it on the basis of what is more useful to them. Written from custody, with execution a live possibility.

2.t: Probably an early hymn Paul is quoting. It describes Christ as existing in the form of God, not grasping at equality, emptying himself, obeying to the point of the cross, and then being exalted and given the name above every name.
Paul applies Isaiah 45:23 — an oath Jehovah swears by himself, that to him every knee will bow — directly to Jesus. That transfer is one of the strongest Christological moves in the New Testament.

2.h: Work out, because God works in
2.t: The two halves must be held together. Our effort is real and it is the evidence of God's prior working, not an alternative to it.

3.t: Paul lists his credentials — the best available — and then uses a deliberately coarse word for what he now considers them. The righteousness he wants is not his own but comes through faith.

3.h: Not that I have obtained it
3.t: Immediately after that, he denies having arrived. Assurance and ongoing struggle sit together in the same paragraph.

4.t: Not an instruction to stop feeling anxious but to redirect it — by prayer, with thanksgiving. The promised result is peace guarding the heart, not the removal of the circumstance.
Contentment is described as learned rather than natural, and in both directions — plenty as well as want. Verse 13 is about enduring circumstances, not achieving ambitions.

1.ctx: Paul started the church in Philippi about AD 49–50, on his second missionary journey (Acts 16). Its first members included Lydia, a businesswoman who traded in purple cloth, and the town jailer and his family. Timothy was with Paul then. Some years later Paul writes this letter from prison.
1.mean: Letters in Paul’s day began with the writer’s name, then the readers’, then a greeting. Paul follows that pattern but fills it with Christian meaning. He calls himself and Timothy ‘servants’ of Christ Jesus. The Greek word means a slave: someone who belongs completely to a master. In most of his letters Paul reminds his readers that he is an apostle, but not here; this church trusted him and there was nothing to defend. He writes to ‘all the saints’. In the Bible a saint is not a specially good Christian but every believer, someone God has set apart for himself because they belong to Christ. He also greets the church’s leaders: the overseers, who led and taught, and the deacons, who served in practical ways. Instead of the usual ‘greetings’, Paul wishes them grace, which is God’s kindness that we do not deserve, and peace, the wholeness that comes from being at peace with God. Both come from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ, named side by side.
1.big: Every believer is a saint, set apart for God in Christ, and grace and peace come to us from the Father and the Son together.
1.diff: Overseers and deacons. ‘Overseers’ (Greek episkopoi, the word that later became ‘bishops’) are plural here, in one church. Calvin concluded that in the New Testament ‘the name of bishop is common to all the ministers of the Word’: overseer, elder and pastor are names for the same office (compare Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7). The New Bible Dictionary agrees that the terms are ‘synonymous in the NT’. Presbyterian, Baptist and many other churches follow this pattern. Catholic teaching holds that ‘the bishops have by divine institution taken the place of the apostles as pastors of the Church’ (Catechism 862), and Orthodox and Anglican churches also keep bishops as a distinct order. The earliest writings after the New Testament are read both ways. Ignatius, writing about AD 110, told the church at Smyrna to ‘follow the bishop’ and to honour ‘the presbytery’ and the deacons. Polycarp, himself bishop of Smyrna, wrote to Philippi telling them to be subject to ‘the presbyters and deacons’, without mentioning a bishop there.

b: Paul calls himself a ‘servant’ (literally ‘slave’, Greek doulos). In 2:7 he uses the same word of Christ, who took ‘the form of a servant’. The church’s leader takes the same lowly place his Lord took, and that is the pattern the whole letter commends.

l.t: How the church began: Lydia by the river, a slave girl set free, and the jailer and his household.
Paul calls a church with serious problems hagioi, ‘saints’ (BSB ‘holy’). Holiness begins as God’s act of setting people apart.
What overseers (elders) and deacons should be like.

Paul names one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, side by side. Naming Jesus with the Father as the giver of grace and peace quietly places him on God’s side, a point the letter makes openly in 2:6–11.

qs: What does Paul call himself, and what does he call the Philippians?
If every believer is a ‘saint’, what does that word say about who you are, and what does it not mean?
Paul greets the leaders alongside everyone else. What does that suggest about how leaders and members should see each other?

1.ctx: The Philippians had supported Paul with money from the very start (4:15–16), and had just sent another gift with Epaphroditus. Letters of the time often moved from the greeting to thanks and prayer.
1.mean: Paul thanks God every time he thinks of the Philippians, and he prays for them with joy. The reason is their ‘partnership in the gospel’. From the first day they have shared in spreading the good news about Jesus: giving money, praying and standing with him, even now that he is in chains. Paul is sure that God, who began this good work in them, will keep at it until it is finished on ‘the day of Christ’, the day Jesus returns. So his confidence does not rest on the Philippians’ strength but on God’s faithfulness. Then he tells them what he prays for them. He asks that their love will keep growing, and growing wiser: love that understands, that can tell what really matters and choose the best, not just what is acceptable. The aim is that they will be pure and blameless when Christ comes, full of the good things a right relationship with God produces. All of it comes through Jesus Christ, and all of it brings praise to God.
1.big: Paul’s confidence rests on God’s faithfulness to finish his work; meanwhile he prays for love that grows in wisdom and goodness.
1.diff: Verse 6 and whether believers can fall away. Reformed theology cites this verse for the perseverance of the saints: those God has truly begun to save ‘can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace’ (Westminster Confession 17.1). Calvin: ‘God does not forsake the work which his own hands have begun.’ Arminian (Wesleyan) readers take the verse as Paul’s confidence in God’s faithfulness to a church that is plainly continuing in faith (their ongoing partnership is the evidence, verses 5 and 7). God will not give up on his work, but a believer can still turn away from him, which is why the New Testament warns against falling away (for example Hebrews 3:12–14). Wesley read the verse as God carrying on his work ‘till it issue in glory’. Both views agree that Paul’s confidence rests on God, not on the Philippians.

b: ‘Partnership’ translates koinōnia, often rendered ‘fellowship’. For Paul it is not a warm feeling but a shared life and shared work. Here it includes the money they gave so the gospel could go forward (4:15).

l.t: The chain of God’s saving work: those he called and justified, he also glorified.
‘The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it.’
The prophets spoke of ‘the day of the LORD’, when God comes to judge and to save. Paul calls it ‘the day of Christ’, giving Jesus the place the LORD has in those passages.
Paul uses the same Greek phrase in Romans 2:18 for approving what is superior, and a similar one in Romans 12:2 for testing and approving God’s will.
The churches of Macedonia, Philippi among them, gave generously out of deep poverty.
The ‘fruit of righteousness’ grows from being joined to Christ.

qs: What is Paul confident about in verse 6, and what is that confidence based on?
Paul prays that love will grow ‘in knowledge and depth of insight’. Why does love need wisdom?
Who has been a partner in the gospel with you? How could you thank God for them, and pray for them, this week?

1.ctx: The Philippians were worried about Paul in prison, and he reassures them. The ‘palace guard’ were soldiers; see the drop-down below.
1.mean: You might expect a missionary in prison to feel that his work had been stopped. Paul says the opposite: his chains have helped the gospel. The soldiers who guard him now know he is a prisoner because of Christ, not because of a crime, and the news has spread. Other believers, seeing his courage, have become bolder in speaking about Jesus. Not all of them have good motives. Some preach out of envy and rivalry, hoping to make things harder for Paul while he is locked up. Others preach out of love. Paul’s response is striking: what matters is that Christ is being preached, so he rejoices either way. These rivals were preaching the true message for the wrong reasons. Paul is very different with people who change the message itself (3:2; Galatians 1:8–9). He expects that through the Philippians’ prayers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus, all this will turn out for his good. His one hope is that Christ will be honoured through him, whether he lives or dies.
1.big: God can use hard circumstances, and even people with mixed motives, to spread the good news; what matters most is that Christ is made known.

b: Verse 19 quotes the Greek Old Testament of Job 13:16 word for word (English translations of Job, made from the Hebrew, word it differently). Job, suffering unjustly, was sure God would one day show he was in the right. Commentators debate whether Paul’s ‘deliverance’ means release from prison, being proved right, or final salvation; either way he borrows Job’s trust that God will vindicate his servant.

l.t: Paul’s words in verse 19 match the Greek translation of this verse exactly.
Paul in chains again, and the word of God still free.
Under guard in Rome, Paul went on preaching boldly.
Joseph: what others meant for harm, God meant for good.
God works all things together for the good of those who love him; Paul is living proof of it in a prison cell.
Jesus’ disciples wanted to stop a man driving out demons in Jesus’ name. ‘For whoever is not against us is for us.’

qs: List the good things Paul says have come from his imprisonment.
Why can Paul rejoice when some people preach Christ to hurt him? Where would he draw the line?
Think of a hard situation you are in. How might Christ be made known through it?

b: The Greek word is praitōrion (BSB footnote: ‘Or all the Praetorium’), from the Latin praetorium. It first meant a general’s headquarters, then a governor’s residence (Mark 15:16; Acts 23:35). It could also mean the soldiers of the Praetorian Guard, the emperor’s elite troops. If Paul was in Rome, these were the soldiers who guarded prisoners awaiting the emperor’s judgement. Some praetorian soldiers are known to have served in the provinces, so some scholars think the word could fit an Ephesian imprisonment too. Either way, Paul’s chained guards were hearing the gospel.

1.ctx: Paul is waiting for a verdict that could mean execution.
1.mean: Paul now thinks aloud about living and dying. ‘For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.’ His whole life is about Christ: knowing him, serving him and making him known. So death cannot rob him of anything; it would only bring him closer to Christ. If he goes on living, that means more useful work. If he dies, he will be with Christ, which he calls far better. He honestly does not know which to prefer. But he decides that, for the Philippians’ sake, it is more necessary for him to stay, and he is confident that he will, so that their faith can grow and their joy increase when he visits them again. Notice what drives his choice. It is not fear of death, nor love of life for its own sake, but what is best for other people.
1.big: For someone whose life is Christ, death is gain, and life is an opportunity to serve others.
1.diff: What happens when a believer dies? Most Christians read verse 23 as showing that believers go to be with Christ at once when they die, awaiting the resurrection of the body (see the key word intermediate state). The Westminster Confession: ‘the souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens’ (32.1). Calvin said this passage sets aside ‘the mad fancy of those who dream that souls sleep when separated from the body’. Catholic teaching agrees that the soul lives on, and adds that some need purification first (see the note on 1 Corinthians 3:10). Seventh-day Adventists and some other groups hold that ‘death is an unconscious state for all people’ until the resurrection; on that view Paul’s words would mean passing straight from death to Christ’s return, since the dead are unaware of the time between. Most Christians reply that ‘far better’ suggests conscious enjoyment of Christ’s presence (compare 2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43).

b: Paul holds two things together. The believer who dies goes to be with Christ, and that is ‘far better’. But the final hope is still the resurrection of the body when Christ returns (3:20–21). Being with Christ now is wonderful; being raised with him is the goal.

l.t: Paul would rather be ‘away from the body and at home with the Lord’.
Jesus to the dying criminal: ‘today you will be with Me in Paradise.’
‘Christ lives in me’; ‘Christ, who is your life’. The same conviction as ‘to live is Christ’.
Jesus: ‘I am the resurrection and the life.’
Death has lost its sting because of Christ’s victory.

qs: Finish Paul’s sentence for yourself: ‘For to me, to live is …’ What would honestly go in the gap?
Why does Paul call dying ‘gain’ and ‘far better’? What does that tell us about life after death?
Paul chooses what is best for others. Where might God be asking you to put others’ needs ahead of your own preferences?

1.ctx: Philippi was a Roman colony, and its people were proud to be Roman citizens (see the history drop-down in the introduction). The Greek word Paul uses for ‘conduct yourselves’ means ‘live as citizens’. Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed in Philippi (Acts 16:22–24).
1.mean: Whatever happens to Paul, the Philippians have a job to do: live in a way that matches the good news about Christ. Paul’s word suggests citizenship. Just as Philippi’s people lived by Rome’s laws and were proud of it, Christians are to live as citizens of God’s kingdom. Here that means two things. First, unity: they are to stand firm together, working side by side like a team for the faith. Second, courage: they must not be frightened by those who oppose them. Their fearlessness is itself a sign. It shows the opponents are on the road to ruin, and it shows the believers that God is saving them. Then Paul says something surprising. God has given them two gifts: not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for him. Suffering for Christ is not a sign that God has left them; it is part of belonging to him. They are in the same struggle they once watched Paul go through in Philippi, and now hear he is still facing.
1.big: Christians live as citizens of heaven: united, unafraid, and willing to suffer for Christ, which is a privilege rather than a defeat.
1.diff: Paul calls both believing and suffering things that are ‘granted’, that is, given as gifts. Reformed theology cites verse 29 to show that faith itself is God’s gift to those he saves. Arminian theology agrees that faith is made possible by grace, but holds that people can resist that grace. Wesley read the verse as ‘a special token of God’s love, and of your being in the way of salvation’.

l.t: Live worthy of your calling, keeping the unity of the Spirit.
What the Philippians ‘saw’ Paul go through: beaten with rods and put in the stocks.
The apostles rejoiced that they had been counted worthy to suffer for Jesus’ name.
Jesus and Peter both call suffering for Christ a blessing.
Saved by grace through faith, and ‘this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God’. Whether ‘this’ means faith itself or the whole of salvation is debated; see Where readings differ.
Paul returns to the citizenship idea: ‘our citizenship is in heaven’.

qs: What two things does Paul say a life ‘worthy of the gospel’ looks like here?
In what sense is suffering for Christ ‘granted’, a gift?
Where do you find it hardest to stand with other Christians, or to be unafraid of opposition?

2.ctx: There were tensions in the church; two leading women had fallen out (4:2). Paul appeals for unity before giving his greatest example.
2.mean: Paul builds his appeal on what the Philippians already have. ‘If’ here really means ‘since’: they do have encouragement from belonging to Christ, comfort from his love, a shared life in the Holy Spirit, and tenderness and compassion. So, Paul says, make my joy complete by living in harmony: thinking along the same lines, loving one another, united in heart and aim. Then he names the enemies of unity. Selfish ambition is the drive to get ahead or to win. Empty pride is wanting to look important. The cure is humility: treating other people as more important than yourself. That does not mean pretending you have no gifts or that your needs do not matter. Paul says to look ‘not only’ to your own interests, but also to the interests of others. Humility means taking your eyes off yourself and paying attention to what others need.
2.big: Unity grows from humility: caring about other people’s good as much as your own.

b: The four ‘if’ phrases in verse 1 describe what God has already given: Christ’s encouragement and love, and fellowship with the Spirit. Church unity is not something Christians create by effort alone; it is living out what God has already made them.

l.t: Honour one another above yourselves, and live in harmony.
Love is not self-seeking.
Carry one another’s burdens.
Greatness in Jesus’ kingdom means serving, as he came to serve. This leads straight into Philippians 2:5–11.
Jesus prayed that his followers would be one, so that the world would believe.

qs: What four things does Paul say the Philippians already have (verse 1)?
What is the difference between humility and simply thinking badly of yourself?
Whose interests could you look out for this week, at home, at work or in church?

2.ctx: Paul gives the supreme example of the humility he has just described. These verses may be an early Christian hymn; see the drop-down below.
2.mean: Paul says: think the way Christ Jesus thought. Then he tells Christ’s story in two movements, down and then up. Down first. Before he was born as a man, Christ already existed ‘in the form of God’: he was truly God, sharing God’s nature and glory. Yet he did not treat being equal with God as something to cling to or use for his own advantage. Instead he ‘emptied Himself’. That does not mean he stopped being God. He laid aside his rights and his glory by taking on something new: the nature of a servant, a real human life. And he went lower still. He obeyed his Father all the way to death, and not an ordinary death but crucifixion, the most shameful death the Roman world knew, used for slaves and rebels. Then up. Because of this, God lifted him to the highest place and gave him ‘the name above all names’. One day every being, in heaven, on earth and under the earth, will bow at the name of Jesus and declare that Jesus Christ is Lord, and this will bring glory to God the Father. The point for the Philippians is this: in God’s kingdom the way up is the way down. If the Son of God stooped that low for others, his people can let go of rivalry and serve one another.
2.big: Christ, who was truly God, stooped to become a servant and die on a cross, and God has exalted him as Lord of all; his people are to share his humble mind.
2.diff: ‘The form of God’. The historic churches read verse 6 as saying Christ truly was God before he became man. Calvin: ‘The form of God means here his majesty’, and he said the passage refutes ‘the impiety of the Arians’, who taught Christ was a created being. Wesley: equality with God was Christ’s ‘own strict and unquestionable right.’ Jehovah’s Witnesses, who do not believe Jesus is Almighty God, translate verse 6: he ‘did not even consider the idea of trying to be equal to God.’ Most translators and scholars reject this, because the verse says he already existed ‘in the form of God’ and the contrast is with what he humbly chose not to hold on to. ‘Emptied Himself’. What did he empty himself of? The historic answer is that the Son did not stop being God, but added a human nature and laid aside the display of his glory and the privileges of his rank. Calvin: he laid aside his glory ‘not by lessening it, but by concealing it.’ Wesley wrote that he emptied himself ‘Of that divine fulness, which he received again at his exaltation.’ In the 19th century some theologians (the ‘kenotic’ theory, from the Greek ekenosen, ‘emptied’) argued that the Son gave up divine attributes such as knowing everything, to take seriously his real human limits (compare Mark 13:32). The New Bible Dictionary judges that this is ‘an entire misunderstanding of the scriptural words’, which are explained by what follows: he emptied himself by ‘taking the form of a servant’. The Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) confessed Christ as one person ‘in two natures’, with ‘the distinction of natures being by no means taken away by the union.’ Every knee shall bow. In Isaiah 45:23 the LORD says, ‘Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance’. Paul applies these words to Jesus. As Gordon Fee argues (as cited in the Lexham Bible Dictionary), ‘the name above all names’ can hardly be anything other than God’s own name.

b: Verses 10–11 take their words from Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD says that every knee will bow before him. In Isaiah this honour belongs to the one true God alone (45:21–22). Paul gives it to Jesus, and says it is ‘to the glory of God the Father’, not at his expense. This is one of the clearest places where the first Christians, Jews committed to one God, worshipped Jesus as Lord.

Some interpreters also see a contrast with Adam. Adam, made in God’s image, grasped at being ‘like God’ (Genesis 3:5) and fell. Christ, who truly was in the form of God, did not grasp, and was exalted. Others think the passage is mainly about Christ’s existence before he became man, and that the Adam contrast is at most in the background.

l.t: The LORD alone is God and Saviour, and every knee will bow to him. Paul applies these words to Jesus.
The LORD’s servant suffers and dies for others, and is then raised and highly exalted: the same down-then-up shape.
The Word was God and became flesh; Jesus speaks of the glory he had with the Father before the world existed.
‘Though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor’.
Knowing he had come from God, Jesus took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet: the mind of Christ in action.
Some see an intended contrast with Adam, who grasped at being like God; others doubt it (see above).
Crowned with glory because he suffered death; he endured the cross and sat down at God’s right hand. See also the key words incarnation and trinity.

qs: Trace the downward steps Christ took in verses 6–8, and the upward steps in verses 9–11.
What do you think ‘emptied Himself’ means? What did Christ give up, and what did he keep?
Paul gives this as an example (verse 5). Where could you go down for someone else’s good this week?

b: Many scholars think verses 6–11 were an early Christian hymn or poem that Paul quotes, because of its rhythm, unusual words and the absence of some typical Pauline themes. Others argue that Paul wrote it himself: he uses unusual words elsewhere, writes rhythmically elsewhere, and need not mention all his themes in one passage. Either way it is very early, written within about 30 years of the crucifixion, and it already speaks of Jesus as existing ‘in the form of God’ before becoming human, and as receiving the worship Isaiah 45:23 reserves for the LORD.

‘Philippians, Letter to the’ and ‘Philippians, Letter to the, Critical Issues’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Fee, Pauline Christology)
Mark J. Keown, Philippians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham Press), via Logos

2.ctx: ‘Therefore’ links back to Christ’s obedience (2:8). Paul is far away and may die, so the Philippians must keep going without him. A drink offering was wine poured out alongside a sacrifice (Numbers 15:5–10).
2.mean: Because Christ obeyed, the Philippians should keep obeying too, even with Paul away. ‘Work out your salvation’ does not mean work to earn it. They already belong to God; Paul is telling them to live out the salvation God has begun and will complete, to let it show in every part of life, and to take that seriously, ‘with fear and trembling’, with deep respect for God. And they can, because God himself is at work in them, giving them both the desire and the power to do what pleases him. Our effort and God’s work are not rivals: God’s work is the reason our effort is possible. One practical test follows: do everything without grumbling or arguing. Israel grumbled in the wilderness; God’s people now should be different. Then they will shine like stars in a dark and twisted world as they hold out the message that gives life. Paul ends with a picture from worship. His life may soon be poured out like a drink offering, a final gift added to their faith and service. Even so he is glad, and he wants them to be glad with him.
2.big: Believers work hard at living out their salvation because God himself is at work in them; lives without grumbling shine in a dark world.
2.diff: God’s work and ours. How the two relate is debated. Reformed: God’s work comes first and is decisive; even our wanting to do good is his doing. Calvin: Paul ‘declares this to be a work of God, without any reservation.’ Arminian (Wesleyan): God’s grace enables and prompts us, and we must respond and cooperate. Wesley: God’s ‘influences are not to supersede, but to encourage, our own efforts.’ Catholic teaching likewise speaks of grace that comes first and of the believer’s free cooperation. All agree that the Christian life involves real effort and that the power for it comes from God.

b: Verse 15’s ‘crooked and perverse generation’ comes from the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:5), where it describes unfaithful Israel. And the word for ‘complaining’ is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel’s grumbling in the wilderness. Paul is saying: you are God’s people on a journey, like Israel; do not repeat their mistakes.

l.t: Moses’ words about a crooked and perverse generation (BSB footnote).
Israel’s grumbling in the wilderness, which Paul also recalls in 1 Corinthians 10:10.
Saved by grace and not by works, yet created in Christ for good works: the same balance as verses 12–13.
God promised to put his Spirit within his people and move them to keep his ways: God at work in us to will and to act.
Believers as lights in the world; the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens.
Near the end of his life Paul again speaks of being poured out like a drink offering.

qs: What do you think Paul means by ‘work out your salvation’, and why does he add ‘with fear and trembling’?
How do verses 12 and 13 fit together: our work and God’s work?
Where are grumbling and arguing most likely to creep into your life, and what would shining look like there?

src.l: Calvin on Philippians 2:12–16, CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Philippians 2
Council of Trent, Session 6 (1547), chs. 5 and 7, in Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 2
Mark J. Keown, Philippians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham Press), via Logos

2.ctx: Epaphroditus had brought the Philippians’ gift to Paul and stayed to help him, but fell dangerously ill. Paul is sending him home, probably carrying this letter.
2.mean: Paul now gives two living examples of the humble, others-first mind he has just described. First, Timothy. Paul hopes to send him soon, because no one else cares so genuinely about the Philippians. Others, Paul says sadly, look after their own interests rather than Jesus Christ’s. Timothy has proved himself, serving with Paul like a son working alongside his father. Second, Epaphroditus, the Philippians’ own messenger. Paul honours him with three titles: brother, fellow worker and fellow soldier. He had been so ill that he nearly died while serving Paul. God had mercy on him, and spared Paul the grief of losing him. Now Epaphroditus is upset because he knows his church heard he was ill, so Paul is sending him home. They are to welcome him with joy and to honour people like him, who risk their lives for Christ’s work. Notice too that God did not simply heal him at once, and that Paul was anxious and expected sorrow. Trusting God does not mean pretending not to feel.
2.big: Faithful, unglamorous service like Timothy’s and Epaphroditus’s is the mind of Christ in action, and deserves honour.

b: ‘Their own interests’ in verse 21 picks up 2:4, and Timothy’s genuine care is the opposite. Paul’s examples run in a line: Christ (2:5–11), then Paul himself (2:17), Timothy and Epaphroditus. The Greek verb for Timothy’s care in verse 20 is the same one Paul uses in 4:6, ‘Be anxious for nothing’. Caring about others is good; it is worry that will not bring things to God that Paul warns against. And when Paul calls Epaphroditus ‘your messenger’ (verse 25), the Greek word is apostolos: he was the church’s sent representative.

l.t: Timothy joined Paul at Lystra; Paul calls him his beloved and faithful child in the Lord.
Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus: even apostles did not always see the sick healed.
Prisca and Aquila risked their lives for Paul, and he honours them by name.
Paul’s daily concern for all the churches: he felt real pressure and care.
Greatness through service; these two men live it out.

qs: What do Timothy and Epaphroditus have in common with the picture of Christ in 2:5–11?
Paul was anxious and expected sorrow even though he trusted God. What does that teach about faith and feelings?
Who are the unnoticed servants in your church? How could you honour them?

3.ctx: A sudden change of tone. Paul warns against teachers, probably Jewish Christians, who insisted that non-Jewish believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God’s people, like those he opposed in Galatia. ‘Dogs’ was an insult some Jews used for Gentiles; Paul turns it back on these teachers.
3.mean: Paul warns the church sharply. Some teachers were saying that to be truly right with God, believers had to be circumcised. Paul calls them dogs and ‘mutilators of the flesh’: their cutting of the body is no longer the mark of God’s people. The true people of God, he says, are those who worship by God’s Spirit, who boast in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in human credentials. Then he shows he is not jealous of what these teachers have. If anyone could trust in religious background and effort, it was Paul. He was circumcised as a baby and born an Israelite, from the tribe of Benjamin. He was a Pharisee who kept the law strictly. He was so zealous that he hunted down Christians. By the law’s standards, no one could find fault with him. But when he met Christ, he counted all of that as loss, even as rubbish, compared with knowing Christ. He no longer relies on a goodness of his own, earned by keeping the law. Instead he wants ‘the righteousness from God’ that comes through faith in Christ: being accepted by God because of Christ, as a gift. His goal now is to know Christ more and more: the power of his resurrection, sharing in his sufferings, becoming like him in his death, and finally rising from the dead.
3.big: Paul gave up every claim to his own goodness to gain Christ, and the righteousness God gives freely through faith.
3.diff: ‘The righteousness from God’. Lutheran and Reformed Christians read verse 9 as a clear statement that believers are accepted by God on the basis of a righteousness that is not their own but is given to them in Christ through faith. Calvin: ‘faith presents man before God as naked, that he may be clothed with the righteousness of Christ.’ Wesley also stressed that it comes ‘by faith alone’, but read verse 9 mainly as the ‘inward righteousness’ the Spirit gives, adding that Paul ‘is far from speaking of justification only’. Catholic teaching, at the Council of Trent, holds that the righteousness by which we are justified is God’s gift, but is a righteousness truly given to and dwelling in the believer: ‘not that whereby he himself is just, but that whereby he maketh us just’. ‘Faith in Christ’ may also be translated ‘the faithfulness of Christ’ (BSB footnote); see the note on Galatians 2:15.

b: ‘It is we who are the circumcision’: even in the Old Testament God wanted circumcised hearts, not only bodies (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4). Paul says this is what the Spirit does in everyone who trusts Christ (Romans 2:28–29; Colossians 2:11). In Greek, Paul’s ‘mutilation’ (katatomē) is a deliberate play on ‘circumcision’ (peritomē).
Verse 9 is one of the New Testament’s clearest descriptions of justification: a right standing with God that is not our achievement but God’s gift, received by faith.

l.t: Israel sought to set up its own righteousness instead of submitting to God’s; Christ is the end of the law for righteousness.
God made the sinless Christ to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
Paul’s own account of his strict upbringing and his persecution of the church.
The man who sells everything for the hidden treasure: counting all as loss to gain Christ.
Joined to Christ in his death and in his resurrection.
Paul’s fuller argument against requiring circumcision.

qs: List the things Paul once trusted in (verses 5–6). What might the modern equivalents be?
What is the difference between ‘my own righteousness’ and ‘the righteousness from God’?
Is there anything you are tempted to count on, apart from Christ, to make you acceptable to God?

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Philippians 3
Council of Trent, Session 6 (1547), chs. 5 and 7, in Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 2

3.ctx: Paul has just spoken of knowing Christ and of the resurrection. Some in the church may have thought they had already arrived spiritually. He uses the picture of a runner in a race.
3.mean: Paul does not want anyone to think he has already reached the finish. He has not yet received all that Christ has for him, and he has not been made perfect. So he keeps pressing on, like a runner leaning toward the tape, to take hold of the prize for which Christ first took hold of him. Notice the order: Christ grabbed hold of Paul first, and that is why Paul runs. There is one thing he does: he forgets what lies behind and strains toward what is ahead. That does not mean wiping his memory. It means refusing to let past failures, or past achievements, hold him back. His eyes are on the prize: God’s heavenly calling in Christ, which will be complete when he is raised and made like Christ. Mature Christians, Paul says, will think this way. If some see things differently, God will make it clear to them. Meanwhile everyone should keep living by what they have already understood.
3.big: The Christian life is a race toward a prize, run by people who know they have not yet arrived and who were first taken hold of by Christ.
3.diff: Perfection. Paul says he has not been ‘made perfect’, yet in verse 15 calls some ‘mature’ (the same Greek root). Wesley taught ‘Christian perfection’, a love for God that can fill the heart in this life while the believer still grows; he noted ‘There is a difference between one that is perfect, and one that is perfected.’ Reformed and Lutheran theology hold that sin remains in believers until death, and read this passage as showing that even Paul never claimed to have arrived.

l.t: Run in such a way as to win the prize.
Run with endurance, with your eyes fixed on Jesus.
At the end of his life Paul has finished the race, and a crown is waiting.
We are not yet without sin, but when Christ appears we will be like him.
Having begun by the Spirit, we do not finish by our own effort.
God’s goal is to make his people like his Son; that is the prize Paul runs toward.

qs: What does Paul admit he has not yet reached?
What do you think ‘forgetting what is behind’ means? What might it not mean?
What from your past, failures or achievements, tends to hold you back from pressing on?

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Philippians 3
Mark J. Keown, Philippians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham Press), via Logos

3.ctx: Philippi’s citizens were proud to belong to Rome, though Rome was far away. Paul uses the idea again (compare 1:27).
3.mean: Paul invites the Philippians to follow his example, and the example of others who live the same way. He needs to, because many live as ‘enemies of the cross of Christ’. He does not name them, and scholars debate who they were; many think his description fits people who live for their appetites and take pride in things they should be ashamed of, while others think ‘belly’ and ‘shame’ point to food laws and circumcision. Their minds are fixed on earthly things, and their end is ruin. Paul says this with tears, not with a sneer. Then comes the contrast: ‘our citizenship is in heaven’. Just as Philippi belonged to Rome though it was far away, believers belong to heaven while they live here. And we eagerly wait for a Saviour from heaven, the Lord Jesus Christ. When he comes, he will change our weak, mortal bodies to be like his glorious resurrection body, by the same power that will bring everything under his rule.
3.big: Believers belong to heaven and wait for their Saviour, who will transform their bodies to be like his.

b: ‘Our citizenship is in heaven’ does not mean Christians are simply waiting to escape to heaven. Paul says the Saviour comes from heaven to us, and the hope is a transformed body. Heaven is our true home country now, and it shapes how we live here.

l.t: God placed everything under the feet of humanity. Paul’s words about Christ bringing all things under his rule echo this psalm, which he also applies to Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:27.
The resurrection body: raised imperishable and glorious.
When Christ appears, we will be like him.
God’s people as strangers looking for a better, heavenly country.
No longer foreigners but fellow citizens with God’s people.
People who serve their own appetites rather than Christ.

qs: How does Paul describe the enemies of the cross, and how does he feel about them?
What difference does it make to know that your citizenship is in heaven?
What would change in your week if your mind were set less on earthly things?

src.l: Calvin on Philippians 3:18–21, CCEL
‘Philippi’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)
Mark J. Keown, Philippians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham Press), via Logos

4.h: Stand Firm, and Agree in the Lord
4.ctx: Euodia and Syntyche were women who had worked alongside Paul in spreading the gospel. Their disagreement was serious enough to mention by name in a letter read aloud to the whole church.
4.mean: Paul speaks with great warmth: these believers are his joy and his crown, the reward he will be glad of when Christ comes. So, he says, stand firm in the Lord in the way he has described. Then he names a problem. Two women, Euodia and Syntyche, have fallen out. Paul does not take sides or tell us what the quarrel was about. In Greek he repeats ‘I urge’ for each of them, and he asks both to ‘agree with each other in the Lord’. Literally that is ‘think the same way’, the very verb he used in 2:2 and 2:5 for sharing the mind of Christ. He asks a trusted helper, his ‘true yokefellow’, to help them make peace. And he honours them: they had fought side by side with him for the gospel, along with Clement and others, and their names are in the Book of Life. People who have served well can still fall out, and those whose names are written in heaven should work to find peace on earth.
4.big: Believers who share the mind of Christ, and whose names are in the Book of Life, must work to make peace with one another.

l.t: Jesus’ instructions to seek reconciliation quickly and directly.
Paul names many women who worked hard in the Lord: Phoebe, Prisca, Mary, Tryphena, Tryphosa and Persis.
The church at Philippi began with women praying by the river.
‘rejoice that your names are written in heaven’: the Book of Life.
God’s book of his people in the Old Testament.
Paul calls another church his joy and crown at Christ’s coming.

qs: How does Paul handle the disagreement between Euodia and Syntyche? What does he not do?
Why might Paul mention that their names are in the Book of Life?
Is there a broken relationship with another Christian that you need to help mend, or to ask for help to mend?

b: Some early Christian writers identified the Clement of 4:3 with Clement, the leader of the church in Rome at the end of the 1st century (the author of 1 Clement). The name was common and the dates are uncertain, so this cannot be confirmed. The ‘true yokefellow’ is unknown. The Greek word may even be a man’s name, Syzygus (BSB footnote), in which case Paul may be playing on its meaning. An old suggestion that it was Paul’s wife was rejected by Calvin, among others.

4.ctx: Paul gives a run of short commands, the kind of closing advice found near the end of several of his letters (compare 1 Thessalonians 5:16–22).
4.mean: Paul’s first command is to rejoice in the Lord, always, and he repeats it in case they missed it. This is not putting on a happy face. It is joy rooted in the Lord, which Paul has even in prison. Next, let everyone see your gentleness: a patient, reasonable spirit that does not insist on its rights. ‘The Lord is near’ may mean that his return is close, or that he is close beside us now; both are true. Then comes a promise about worry. Instead of being anxious about anything, bring everything to God in prayer, telling him what you need, and thank him as you do. The result is not that every problem disappears, but that God’s peace, deeper than we can understand, stands guard over our hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. Finally Paul tells them what to fill their minds with: whatever is true, honourable, right, pure, lovely and admirable. They are also to put into practice what they have learned and seen in him. Then the God of peace will be with them.
4.big: Joy in the Lord, gentleness, and prayer instead of worry: the peace of God guards those who bring everything to him.

mis.t: ‘Be anxious for nothing’ is sometimes used to tell people that feeling anxious is a sin, or that an anxiety disorder shows a lack of faith.
mis.b: The same Greek verb describes Timothy’s good ‘care’ for the church (2:20), and Paul admits his own daily ‘concern for all the churches’ (2 Corinthians 11:28). Jesus himself was ‘deeply troubled and distressed’ in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33–34). Paul is not forbidding the feeling; he is telling us what to do with it: bring it to God in prayer, with thanks. We would add that for ongoing anxiety, prayer and practical and professional help belong together.

b: Paul does not explain ‘The Lord is near’. One major commentary notes ‘a remarkable lack of agreement’ over whether he means near in time or near in presence. Both fit Paul’s thought: Christ is coming (3:20), and he is with his people now by his Spirit.

l.t: Jesus’ teaching on worry: your Father knows what you need.
‘Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.’
The LORD is near to all who call on him.
Jesus gives a peace the world cannot give.
God keeps in perfect peace the mind that trusts him.
Set your minds on things above; be transformed by the renewing of your mind.

qs: What does Paul tell us to do instead of being anxious, and what does he promise?
How can joy be commanded? What is the difference between joy in the Lord and simply being happy?
Look at the list in verse 8. What are you feeding your mind on, and what might need to change?

src.l: Calvin on Philippians 4:4–9, CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Philippians 4
Mark J. Keown, Philippians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham Press), via Logos
Rachael Newham, ‘The two most misused Bible verses on mental health’, Premier Christianity (16 May 2024)

4.ctx: Paul thanks the Philippians for the gift Epaphroditus brought. In that culture, giving and receiving gifts was a serious part of friendship, and Paul words his thanks carefully.
4.mean: Paul is delighted that the Philippians have been able to send help again. But he wants them to know that his joy is not because he was desperate. He has learned to be content in every situation, whether he has plenty or very little, whether he eats well or goes hungry. Then comes the famous verse: ‘I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.’ In context, ‘all things’ means coping with every situation, hungry or full, rich or poor. The secret of Paul’s contentment is not his own toughness but Christ’s strength. Still, he does not brush their kindness aside. They did well to share in his troubles. From the very start they were the only church that gave to support him, even when he was in Thessalonica. He is not hinting for more. What he wants is the reward God will credit to their account. Their gift is like a sacrifice with a pleasing smell, an offering God gladly accepts. And the God they have honoured will supply all their needs from his glorious riches in Christ Jesus.
4.big: Contentment comes from Christ’s strength in every circumstance, and God receives generous giving as an offering to him.

mis.t: ‘I can do all things through Christ’ is often quoted as a promise of success: winning the match, passing the exam, getting the job.
mis.b: In context Paul is talking about contentment, being able to live through hunger and plenty alike (verses 11–12). One major commentary notes how often the verse is turned into a promise that Christ will help a believer achieve whatever they set their mind to, and rejects that reading. Christ does give strength for every situation he calls us into; the verse is about enduring with him, not about achieving our own goals. In the same way, ‘my God will supply all your needs’ (verse 19) is said to a church that had just given sacrificially, and it promises needs, not wants.

b: The word for ‘content’ (verse 11) was a favourite of the Stoic and Cynic philosophers, for whom it meant being self-sufficient and needing no one. Paul takes the word and turns it round: his sufficiency is not in himself but in Christ who strengthens him. ‘I have learned the secret’ (verse 12) uses a word for being initiated into a religious mystery. Paul’s secret is not a ritual but a person.

l.t: Godliness with contentment is great gain.
Be content, because God has promised never to leave you.
Christ’s power is made perfect in weakness: when I am weak, then I am strong.
Believers from Macedonia supplied Paul’s needs in Corinth.
‘A fragrant offering’ is Old Testament sacrifice language; Ephesians uses the same phrase for Christ’s death. Generous giving is an offering that echoes the cross.
Doing good and sharing are sacrifices that please God.

qs: What has Paul learned (verses 11–12), and how do you think he learned it?
How does reading verse 13 in its context change what it means?
Where do you find contentment hardest? What would relying on Christ’s strength look like there?

src.l: Calvin on Philippians 4:10–14, CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Philippians 4
Mark J. Keown, Philippians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham Press), via Logos

4.ctx: The closing greetings. ‘The household of Caesar’ were people in the emperor’s service; see the drop-down below.
4.mean: Paul ends by sending greetings to every believer, ‘all the saints’, and passes on greetings from the Christians with him. One group is singled out: believers from ‘the household of Caesar’. This does not mean the emperor’s family, but the large staff of slaves and freed slaves who worked in the emperor’s service and ran much of the empire’s business. The gospel had reached even there, perhaps partly through Paul’s imprisonment (1:13). For the Philippians, proud of their Roman connections, that was good news. Paul closes as he began, with grace: ‘The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.’ The whole letter is held between two mentions of God’s kindness in Christ.
4.big: The gospel had reached even the emperor’s own staff, and grace is the first and last word for God’s people.

l.t: Paul’s chains had made Christ known among the imperial guard.
Paul ends other letters with the same blessing.
Paul greets believers in other great households in Rome.
Grace at the start and at the end: the Christian life begins and ends in God’s kindness.

qs: Who sends greetings, and who is singled out?
Why might it encourage the Philippians that there were believers in Caesar’s household?
Where are the unexpected places the gospel has reached in your workplace or community?

b: ‘Caesar’s household’ does not mean the emperor’s family. A great Roman’s household (familia) included his slaves and freedmen, and the emperor’s household was in effect the civil service of the empire: secretaries, accountants, doctors, managers. Many were Greek-speaking easterners. So it is not surprising to find believers among them. Whether these were in Rome or in an imperial office in a province depends on where Paul was writing.
